title: Access token and rotating refresh token service
name: Agent session tokens

questions.prompt: Is there a defect in how this code issues, rotates and revokes session tokens? If so, mark the line(s) where it is; otherwise answer that there is none.
An attacker replays a refresh token that the legitimate client already rotated. What does the code do?
choices: Issues a second token pair, since the token is still before its expiry time.
Rejects the request and leaves the legitimate client's newer token valid, so only the replay fails.
Rejects the request and revokes every token in that session family, forcing the legitimate client to sign in again.
Rejects the request and deletes only the replayed record from the store.

questions.prompt: Why is rotate annotated with @Transactional(noRollbackFor = InvalidTokenException.class) while the other methods use plain @Transactional?
choices: Because rotate is the only method that reads from the store.
So that the work done before the exception is thrown, namely revoking the family on reuse, is committed instead of rolled back.
So that the new refresh record inserted by issueInFamily survives when the access token cannot be signed.
So that Spring retries the method when an InvalidTokenException occurs.

questions.prompt: An agent's access token has a 15-minute lifetime. Which statement about its verification is true?
choices: A token whose expiry passed 20 seconds ago is still accepted because of the configured clock skew.
A token signed with a different secret but carrying the correct issuer and audience claims is accepted.
A token whose expiry passed 20 seconds ago is rejected because the skew only applies to the not-before claim.
A token with the signature removed and the algorithm set to none is accepted when the claims are valid.
